title: Frank Ferrari's clubs, return to trumpet, and four years with Paul Barbarin
summary: He worked in the French Quarter trio for Ferrari, returned to trumpet as Dixieland revived, and played with Paul Barbarin from 1954 to 1958.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: For Frank Ferrari. So, well, he didn't think much of the idea of hiring a trio, so he, I guess he said, well, I think I'll give him something to do anyhow. So, he wanted to see how eager we was to, to, to hold a job. You understand? Yeah. He thought maybe we'd just go there for food. He said, well, I'll tell you what to do. He said, if you want the job, he said, your job start at 12 o'clock at night, you play at 6 o'clock in the morning. I said, well, all right, we take the job. And we did that for about three months. So, he said, well, these fellas really must want to work, you know? So then, I mean, well, he got kind of close with us, and then he found out that we were a family man, you know? And we, and we, we had to work. I mean, we weren't these adventurous type fellas, you know? So, well, we played, we worked there, then we moved next door to the Three Deucers. That was also his place. And I stayed there three years. See? Three Deucers, and that's how I come to Billy's house. See? Off the Three Deucers. Well, then eventually, well, then the Dixieland bands were starting to come in then. You know, that was around 1950, 49. Dixieland band was just starting to come back in. See, Sharky was very famous then at the famous door. See? So, this happened around 1954 or something like that. I couldn't find nothing to do then. I was out of work, you know? And I couldn't find anything to do. I mean, I was having it kind of rough, because my brother-in-law taught me how to paint, and then the paint work was rough, too. See? So, he encouraged me to pick up the trumpet, because Paul Bobrand didn't need a trumpet player. So, I said, oh, man, no, I never make trumpet. He said, man, I'm telling you. He said, man, I played a job last night. Look at the job. Now, he was telling me a story, but he was telling me that to encourage me. He said, man, look at the job paid for $22, man. We played three hours. Look at that, man. Then he pulled out the money and he showed me. You understand? But he was exaggerating, but at that time, I didn't know it. See? He was doing that to encourage me to get back on the trumpet. See? My brother-in-law, that's the son of the head. Brother-in-law, that's the son of the head. So, well, eventually, he keep talking to me. So, I said, well, I don't know the tunes. He said, well, I'll hum the tunes. And I was sitting out right in that chair where you were sitting that day, right on the table there, and I'd take that trumpet, and he'd hum the tune, and I'd play the notes and everything, and get the division and sit down and wrote all them Dixieland tunes out. And I have them inside right now. See? And wrote all them tunes out. Then, eventually, I got with Paul Barbera. See? So, Paul Hyman. So, I stayed with Paul from 54 until 58 of December. That's four years I stayed with Paul. See? Well, we've been to New York, and we've been to California. Paul, we played, uh, in New York, we played, uh, Paramount, wasn't it?
